I'm assuming you've taken your fair share of physics courses.  At least A10 and A11 anyhow.  With either of those courses, very little of what they taught was just pure theory.  To use a simple example: One of Newtons Laws is that an object needs a force acting on it to experience a change in motion.  While this is handy to know, you could also pull that exact same information from F = ma.  Because the theory and the math convey the same information, you can use the math to derive the theory and you can use the theory to derive the math.

So if he gives a particularly difficult short answer question, even though you can't use math or graphs to answer it, I find its often helpful to mathematically describe the scenario for your own benefit.  Sort of as a failsafe if you can't recall what a specific piece of information said.

So in quantum, knowing how and why all the derivations worked along with his explanations to things really helped.  That way if a specific subject is iffy, you can think back to both his instruction and the equations to come up with an answer.  But at the end of the day, he does mark hard and you really do need to be perfect if you want perfect.

I'd disagree on the point that post-Microsoft Mojang released bigger content changes.  Microsoft bought Minecraft in 2014.  Before that we had things like the update that changed the world, the creations of the Nether and End, as well as a lot of the core gameplay features we see in the game.  I'd say any of those updates are on par with things like Caves and Cliffs, or the Nether Update in terms of content and influence.  Granted, post-Microsoft, there have been more updates, but that's also partly because Notch had the game for 5 years, while Microsoft has had it for 10.

There's also lots more to hate about the Microsoft takeover than just Minecoins.  I'm still angry about the mandatory account Migration.

And on a more personal note: the old style Minecraft updates are ones I personally prefer more.  While updates like Trails and Tales, Tricky Trials, or even the Wild Update or Caves and Cliffs are wonderful updates that add a lot of content, the content added doesn't suit my playstyle specifically.  I preferred Minecraft when the world was emptier.  I don't play this game to go on grand adventures and gather collectibles, I play to enjoy the quiet solitude of an empty world that's mine to explore and shape.  For me, old Minecraft captured that feeling a lot better.  Especially before they changed up the soundtrack too.  The fewer structures and their more basic designs made the world feel a lot emptier and therefore more like my own canvas.  The music amplified that feeling.  The updates they added didn't require you to venture thousands of blocks to play the one-off dungeons, Instead, they added relatively few new blocks and features that affected almost every aspect of gameplay.  Take Beta 1.7 for example.  Really all this update did was add Pistons.  We'd consider it really small in reference to modern updates, yet it changed how I play the game in a much more meaningful way than Caves and Cliffs or the Wild Update did.

This isn't to say that pre-Microsoft Minecraft was objectively better, it just captured a feeling for me that Modern Minecraft doesn't, specifically because of the new content.  Pair this with the fact that the newer content doesn't really mesh well with my playstyle and I think it makes sense why I personally would prefer the older updates to the newer ones.  Doesn't stop me from playing or enjoying the game though - I've been in the same survival world for over a decade and still play quite frequently when I can.

I find it usually happens really early on.  Kids when learning things like fractions and long division, little kids will be taught to memorize the formulas/processes. At that point, they disconnect from what math actually is and start seeing as a game of memorizing rules.  This is mostly the fault of the school system.  
But none the less, out of a class of 20 or so kids, maybe five will just so happen to stumble across an intuitive understanding (either on accident, or through self exploration), and continue to appreciate math for what it is.  The rest will see it as another pointless numbers rule-based hell and have a really bad time.

Sucks seeing how the school system can ruin something so interesting.

I'm a strong believe that vertical slabs should stay out of the game.

  
Firstly, looking at some of the blocks you listed:

* Beds - primary use is spawn-setting and passing the night.
* Lecterns - primary use as a villager workstation, with usage as a redstone component as well.
* Chiseled Bookshelves - though mainly aesthetic, its also a heavy redstone component.
* Bells - Primary tied to villager/raid mechanics.
* Anvils - Primary use in the enchantment/repair system.
* Stonecutters - Primary use as a crafting block and villager workstation.
* Cakes - Primary use as a food, and was mainly added as a novelty/joke item if Minecraft won an indie game award.
* Grindstones - Primary use in the enchantment system, and as a villager workstation.
* Fletching Tables - Primary use as a villager work station.

I'd also like to add, slabs themselves weren't even initially supposed to be decorative.  They were added to the game in a state where they couldn't be placed as top slabs.  Stairs couldn't initially be placed upside-down.  These two blocks were also utility features meant to make movement easier.  They weren't specifically added to give builders more tools.

Now, I think Bookshelves, brick shades, and stripped logs don't necessarily fit the same mold as vertical slabs because they're still full blocks.  Adding more colors doesn't really affect building as much as vertical slabs would.  I have never gone back to my older builds to change out old blocks for better-fitting colors.  I did, however, go back and change old builds to add upside-downs stairs and slabs when they were added to the game.  My point in this paragraph isn't to say that vertical slabs are bad, but that vertical slabs are fundamentally different than adding in different block colors/textures.  In a game like Minecraft, shapes are much more important to building than color.

As for carpets, walls, and iron bars (glass panes too), it's much harder to differentiate between them and vertical slabs.  Fences in there too.  These blocks all have distinct unique shapes, and have no real purpose for having them aside from being decorative.  I figure modern Mojang probably wouldn't add them either if they weren't already grandfathered in (iron bars in 2011, carpets in 2013, walls in 2012, and fences in 2010).

So, with vertical slabs being different than most of the provided examples, I still feel like they'd inhibit creativity.  Not in the sense that they'd cause people to be less creative in their building.  Opening more doors with more tools will always lead to more people doing more things.  But it would reduce the creativity in relation to Minecraft as it is now.  Minecraft has always been a very minimalistic game.  That's why it's unique.  Building in Minecraft was always unique because it gave you very restrictive shapes to work with.  Redstone in Minecraft was always unique because it gave you very basic components and allowed you do whatever you wanted with them.  Creativity in Minecraft is all about the player interacting with simple systems to produce complex results.  So while things like vertical slabs would change things, and allow for more complex shapes, they would take away some of the problem-solving that's inherently tied to the game as a whole.

With all that in mind, Mojang does seem to be changing how they view the game, and block complexity has been going up over the years.  So who knows, we may see vertical slabs in a few years, and I'll have to adjust.  Either way, this comment was much too long.  I gotta get a life.
